result.reason: The passage is the Mishnah text covering chalitza, yibum, and the kohen gadol's prohibition from marrying a widow, which is precisely what the 'Family Law' section prose discusses.

Both items describe the kohen gadol's behavior during a relative's funeral procession — Rabbi Meir's view and Rabbi Yehuda's stricter view — which is precisely what the 'Mourning Rules' prose discusses in detail.

The passage describes the consolation rituals of the kohen gadol — passing in line, 'we are your atonement,' reclining on the ground vs. bench — which is exactly what the 'Consolation Rituals' prose discusses in detail.

The passage covers exactly the restrictions enumerated in candidate 1's prose: the king's exemption from judging/being judged, testimony, ḥalitza, and levirate marriage, including the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the tanna kamma — all of which are discussed in detail under 'King Restrictions'.

The passage directly discusses the prohibition on marrying a king's widow and Rabbi Yehuda's exception allowing a king to marry another king's widow, which is precisely what the 'Royal Marriage' section's prose addresses.

All three items together form the continuous Gemara analysis that heading 0 ('Self-Judgment First') explicitly describes — the obvious/non-obvious question about the kohen gadol judging and being judged, the Resh Lakish derivation, the symmetry with the king passage, and the baraita about the kohen gadol who kills — all of which the prose of heading 0 covers in full detail, while headings 1 and 2 cover only the subsequent analysis of the baraita's exile clause.

Both items discuss the Gemara's reasoning about why a High Priest is exiled despite having no release mechanism (the 'kol de'it lei takanta' argument and its resolution from 'kol rotzeiach'), which is precisely what the 'Permanent Exile' section's prose elaborates upon.

All three items discuss the High Priest being treated as an ordinary person for non-capital transgressions and the textual basis (hadavar hagadol) for limiting the elevated beit din to capital matters, which is precisely what the 'Non-Capital Crimes' prose section discusses.

Both items are the Gemara's challenge from the baraita about 'vehisalamta' and the three exemption cases (kohen/cemetery, elder/dignity, greater work value), which is precisely what candidate 0's prose describes as the setup for questioning whether the High Priest must testify.

Both items together form the continuous chain of objections and revisions around Rav Yosef's statement about the High Priest testifying in connection with a king, which is precisely what heading 0 ('Royal Testimony') introduces — the entire sequence from the initial ruling through the ben melech objection and the final resolution about testifying before the king all belongs to that one discussion, and the current placement under heading 2 splits this natural unit mid-stream.

The passage explicitly discusses the prohibition of seating a king on the Sanhedrin and the derivation from 'lo sa'aneh al riv/rav,' which is exactly what the 'King on Sanhedrin' section's prose addresses.

The passage discusses the disqualification of both the king (due to afsanya) and the High Priest (due to tzina) from leap year intercalation courts, which is precisely what the 'Leap Year Conflicts' section's prose addresses.

Both items together form the opening of the cowherd story — Rav Pappa's inference followed immediately by the challenge from the three cattle herders — which is precisely the content described in the 'Shepherds & Tekufah' section's prose.
